{{Short description|Japanese Inland Sea}} {{more citations needed|date=May 2010}} {{Infobox body of water | name = Seto Inland Sea | image = Seto Inland Sea.jpg | caption = View of the Seto Inland Sea from [[Itsukushima|Miyajima island]] | image_bathymetry = Seto-Inland-Sea-Photo.jpg | caption_bathymetry = The Inland Sea and its major straits | location = [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] | coords = {{coord|34|10|N|133|20|E|region:JP_type:waterbody_scale:1300000|display=inline,title}} | type = [[Sea]] | inflow = |pushpin_map=Japan | outflow = | catchment = | basin_countries = [[:en:Japan|Japan]] | length = | width = | area = {{convert|23203|km2|sqmi|-2|abbr=on}} | depth = {{convert|38|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} | max-depth = | volume = | reference = }} The {{nihongo|'''Seto Inland Sea'''|瀬戸内海|Seto Naikai}}, sometimes shortened to the '''Inland Sea''', is the body of water separating [[Honshu]], [[Shikoku]], and [[Kyushu]], three of the four main islands of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It serves as a [[waterway]] connecting the [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] to the [[Sea of Japan]]. It connects to [[:en:Osaka Bay|Osaka Bay]] and provides a sea transport link to industrial centers in the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]], including [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]] and [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]. Before the construction of the [[San'yō Main Line]], it was the main transportation link between Kansai and Kyūshū. [[Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi]], [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama]], [[:en:Hyōgo Prefecture|Hyōgo]], [[:en:Osaka Prefecture|Osaka]], [[Wakayama Prefecture|Wakayama]], [[:en:Kagawa Prefecture|Kagawa]], [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime]], [[Tokushima Prefecture|Tokushima]], [[:en:Fukuoka Prefecture|Fukuoka]], and [[:en:Ōita Prefecture|Ōita]] prefectures have coastlines on the Seto Inland Sea; the cities of [[:en:Hiroshima|Hiroshima]], [[:en:Iwakuni|Iwakuni]], [[Takamatsu]], and [[:en:Matsuyama|Matsuyama]] are also located on it. The [[Setouchi region]] encompasses the sea and surrounding coastal areas. The region is known for its moderate climate, with a stable year-round temperature and relatively low rainfall levels. The sea is famous for its periodic {{nihongo|[[red tide]]s|赤潮|akashio}} caused by dense groupings of certain [[:en:phytoplankton|phytoplankton]] that result in the death of large numbers of fish. Since the 1980s, the sea's northern and southern shores have been connected by the three routes of the [[:en:Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project|Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project]], including the [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]], which serves both railroad and automobile traffic. ==Extent== The [[:en:International Hydrographic Organization|International Hydrographic Organization]]'s definition of the limits of the Seto Inland Sea (published in 1953) is as follows:{{cite web|url=https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/standards/s-23/S-23_Ed3_1953_EN.pdf|title=Limits of Oceans and Seas, 3rd edition|year=1953|publisher=International Hydrographic Organization|access-date=28 December 2020}}
''On the West.'' The southeastern limit of the Japan Sea [In [[:en:Kanmon Straits|Shimonoseki-kaikyo]]. A line running from Nagoya Saki (130°49'E) in [[Kyushu|Kyûsû]] through the islands of Uma Sima and Muture Simia (33°58',5N) to Murasaki Hana (34°01'N) in [[Honshu|Honsyû]]]. ''On the East ([[:en:Kii Channel|Kii Suidô]]).'' A line running from Takura Saki (34°16'N) in Honsyû to Oishi Hana in the island of [[:en:Awaji Island|Awazi]], through this island to Sio Saki (34°11'N) and on to Oiso Saki in [[Shikoku|Sikoku]]. ''On the South ([[:en:Bungo Channel|Bungo Suidô]]).'' A line joining Sada Misaki (33°20'N) in Sikoku and Seki Saki in Kyûsyû.
The range of the Seto Inland Sea by the Territorial Sea Law ([[:ja:領海及び接続水域に関する法律|領海及び接続水域に関する法律]]) is {{convert|19,700|km2|mi2|abbr=on}}. The range of the Seto Inland Sea according to the Setouchi Law and the Setouchi Law Enforcement Order is {{convert|21,827|km2|mi2|abbr=on}}. ==Geographical features== [[File:Chugoku-Region-Shikoku-Japan-ISS-Space.png|thumb|220px|The Seto Inland Sea with [[Shikoku]] and [[:en:Chūgoku region|Chūgoku]] from the [[:en:International Space Station|ISS]]]] [[File:Setouchi.jpg|thumb|220px|The beauty of the islands of the Seto Inland Sea, [[Suō-Ōshima]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]]] The Seto Inland Sea is 450 km (280 mi) long from east to west. The width from south to north varies from 15 to 55 km (10 to 34 mi). In most places, the water is relatively shallow. The average depth is 38 m (125 ft); the greatest depth is 105 m (344 ft).{{cite web|title=Inland Sea|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/288431/Inland-Sea|publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica Online|access-date=22 February 2013}} Hydrologically, Seto Inland Sea is not a true [[:en:inland sea|inland sea]], being neither an [[:en:epeiric|epeiric]] body of water like [[:en:Hudson Bay|Hudson Bay]] nor an isolated [[:en:endorheic basin|endorheic basin]] like the [[:en:Caspian Sea|Caspian Sea]]. Rather, it is actually a [[:en:marginal sea|marginal sea]]: a division of a wider ocean (in this case the Pacific) which is partially enclosed by islands, archipelagos, or peninsulas (here, the Japanese Home Islands), adjacent to or widely open to the open ocean at the surface. The [[:en:Naruto Strait|Naruto Strait]] connects the eastern part of the Seto Inland Sea to the [[:en:Kii Channel|Kii Channel]], which in turn connects to the Pacific. The western part of the Seto Inland Sea connects to the Sea of Japan through the [[:en:Kanmon Straits|Kanmon Straits]] and to the Pacific through the [[:en:Bungo Channel|Bungo Channel]]. Each part of the Seto Inland Sea has a separate name in Japanese. For example, {{nihongo|''Iyo-nada''|伊予灘}} refers to the strait between Ehime, Yamaguchi, and Ōita prefectures in the western portion of the sea; {{nihongo|''Aki-nada''|安芸灘}} is the open expanse west of the [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]], near Hiroshima prefecture; and {{nihongo|''Suō-nada''|周防灘}} refers to the expanse between Yamaguchi prefecture and [[Suō-Ōshima]]. These areas are sometimes styled Iyonada, Akinada, and Suonada. There are also many straits located between the major islands, as well as a number of smaller ones that pass between islands or connect the Seto Inland Sea to other seas or the [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific]]. Almost 3,000 islands are located in the Seto Inland Sea. The largest island is [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji-shima]], and the second largest is [[Shōdo Island|Shōdo-shima]]. Many of the smaller islands are uninhabited. ===Major islands=== *Eastern part: [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji Island]], [[Shōdo Island]], Ieshima Islands, [[Naoshima]] Islands, [[Shiwaku Islands]], [[Yumeshima]] *Central part: [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]] (including [[:en:Ōmishima|Ōmishima]], [[:en:Innoshima, Hiroshima|Innoshima]]), [[Itsukushima]] (popularly known as Miyajima), [[Hinase Islands]], [[:en:Kasaoka Islands|Kasaoka Islands]] *Western part: [[Suō-Ōshima]], [[Uwakai Islands]], [[:en:Hashira Island|Hashira-jima]] Islands. ==Fauna== Over 500 marine species are known to live in the Seto Inland Sea. Examples are the [[:en:Ayu sweetfish|ayu]], an [[:en:fish migration|amphidromous]] fish, [[:en:horseshoe crab|horseshoe crab]], [[:en:finless porpoise|finless porpoise]], and [[:en:great white shark|great white shark]], which has occasionally attacked people in the Seto Inland Sea. In the past, [[whale]]s entered the sea to feed or breed, however because of [[whaling]] and pollution, they are rarely seen. ==History== [[Image:ItsukushimaTorii7492.jpg|thumb|220px|Seto Inland Sea seen from the [[Torii]] of [[Itsukushima Shrine]]]] During the last [[:en:ice age|ice age]], the [[sea level]] was lower than today. After the ice age, sea water poured into a basin between the [[:en:Chūgoku|Chūgoku]] mountains and [[Shikoku]] mountains and formed the Seto Inland Sea as it is known today. From ancient times, the Seto Inland Sea served as a main transport line between its coastal areas, including what is today the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]] and [[Kyushu]]. It was also a main transport line between Japan and other countries, including Korea and China. Even after the creation of major highways such as the [[:en:Nankaidō|Nankaidō]] and [[San'yōdō]], the Seto Inland Sea remained a major transport route. There are records that some foreign emissaries from China and Korea sailed on the Seto Inland Sea. The importance of water traffic gave rise to private navies in the region. In many documents, these navies were called {{nihongo|''suigun''|水軍||"water army"}}, or simply pirates. Sometimes they were considered to be public enemies, but in most cases they were granted the right to self-governance as a result of their strength. During the feudal period, ''suigun'' seized power in most coastal areas. The Kono in [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo Province]] (today [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime Prefecture]]) and [[:en:Kobayakawa clan|Kobayakawa]] (later [[:en:Mōri clan|Mōri]]) in [[:en:Aki Province|Aki Province]] (today a part of [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]]) clans were two of the more famous ''suigun'' lords. In the 12th century, [[Taira no Kiyomori]] planned to move the capital from [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] to the coastal village of Fukuhara (today [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]) to promote trade between Japan and the [[Song dynasty]] of China. This transfer was unsuccessful, and soon after Kyoto became the capital again. Later, the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] took place off the coast of present-day Takamatsu. In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the Seto Inland Sea was one of the busiest transport lines in Japan. It was a part of a navigational route around Japan's islands via the Sea of Japan. Many ships navigated from its coastal areas to the area along the Sea of Japan. Major ports in the Edo period were Osaka, Sakai, Shimotsui, [[Ushimado]], and Tomonoura. The Seto Inland Sea also served many ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' in the western area of Japan as their route to and from [[:en:Edo|Edo]], to fulfill their obligations under ''[[sankin-kōtai]]''. Many used ships from Osaka. Thanks to transport through the Seto Inland Sea, Osaka became the economic center of Japan. Each [[:en:Han (Japan)|''han'']] had an office called ''Ozakayashiki'' in Osaka. These ''Ozakayashiki'' were among Japan's earliest forms of banks, facilitating domestic trade and helping to organize the income of the ''daimyo'', which was in the form of ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'', giant bales of rice. The Seto Inland Sea was also part of the official Chosendentsushi route, bringing Korean emissaries to the shogunate. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], the coastal cities along the Seto Inland Sea were rapidly industrialized. One of the headquarters of the [[:en:Imperial Japanese Navy|Japanese Navy]] was built in the town of [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure]]. Since the Meiji period, development of land transport has been reducing the importance of the Seto Inland Sea as a transport line. Remarkable land transportation innovations include the [[San'yō Main Line|San'yō Main Railroad Line]] in Honshū and the [[Yosan Main Railroad Line]] in Shikoku (both completed before [[World War II]]) and three series of bridges connecting Honshū and Shikoku (completed in the late 20th century). The Seto Inland Sea is still used, however, by an international cargo transport line and several local transport lines connecting Honshū with Shikoku and Kyūshū. ==Industry== Major cities with heavy industrial activity on the coast of the Seto Inland Sea include Osaka, Kobe, and Hiroshima. Smaller scale manufacturing and industry can also be found in [[:en:Kurashiki|Kurashiki]], [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure]], [[:en:Fukuyama, Hiroshima|Fukuyama]], and [[Ube, Yamaguchi|Ube]] in Honshū, and [[Sakaide, Kagawa|Sakaide]], [[:en:Imabari, Ehime|Imabari]], and [[:en:Niihama|Niihama]] in Shikoku. Major industries include [[steel]] production, vehicle manufacture, ship building, textiles, and since the 1960s, oil refining and chemical products. [[:en:Imabari Shipbuilding|Imabari Shipbuilding]], Japan's largest ship building company, has its headquarters and some of its yards in [[:en:Imabari, Ehime|Imabari, Ehime]] Prefecture. Thanks to the moderate climate and beautiful landscape, fishing, agriculture, and tourism bring a lot of income to the area as well. == Transport == [[Image:Map_of_Honshu-Shikoku_Bridge_Project.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.5|Major highways in the Seto Inland Sea. Yellow: Kobe-Awaji-Naruto. Green: Seto-Ōhashi. Red: [[:en:Nishiseto Expressway|Nishiseto Expressway]].]] [[File:Wake behind a ferry.jpg|thumb|220px|KURE-MATSUYAMA ferry, Seto Inland Sea 2017]] Today the Seto Inland Sea serves its coastal areas mainly for two purposes: first, international or domestic cargo transportation, and second, local transportation between coastal areas and islands on the sea. Major ports are Kobe, Okayama, [[:en:Port of Takamatsu|Takamatsu]], Tokushima, Matsuyama, and Hiroshima. Historically, the Seto Inland Sea as transport line served four coastal areas: Kansai, Chūgoku, Shikoku, and eastern Kyūshū. The Seto Inland Sea provided each of these regions with local transportation and connected each region to the others and far areas, including the coastal area of the Sea of Japan, Korea, and China. After Kobe port was founded in 1868 to serve foreign ships, the Seto Inland Sea became a major international waterway with connection to the Pacific. Development of land transportation shifted the travel between east and west — that is, between Honshū and Kyūshū — to railroad and road transport. Two coastal railways, San'yō Main Line in Honshū and Yosan Main Line, were built. Those railway lines stimulated the local economy and once invoked a rail mania. Many short railroads were planned to connect a certain station of those two lines and a local seaport on the Seto Inland Sea, and some of them were actually built. The Ministry of Railroads, later the [[:en:Japanese National Railways|Japanese National Railways]] and then [[Shikoku Railway Company]], ran some train ferry lines between Honshū and Shikoku including the line between Uno Station (Tamano) and [[Takamatsu Station (Kagawa)|Takamatsu Station]] (Takamatsu). When the [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]] was finished and began to serve the two coastal areas, that ferry line was abolished. ===Highways and bridges=== [[File:Akashi_Bridge.JPG|thumb|220px|right|[[:en:Akashi Kaikyō Bridge|Akashi Kaikyō Bridge]]]] The main islands Honshū and Shikoku are connected by three series of bridges since the late 1980s. This improves land transportation between the connected islands. These series of bridges, collectively known as the [[:en:Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project|Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project]], are, from east to west, [[:en:Akashi Kaikyo Bridge|Akashi Kaikyo Bridge]], [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]], and [[:en:Nishiseto Expressway|Nishiseto Expressway]]. ====Kobe-Awaji-Naruto Highway==== The easternmost highway was built between 1976 and 1998. It leads from [[Akashi,_Hyōgo|Akashi]] ([[:en:Hyōgo Prefecture|Hyōgo Prefecture]]) on the [[:en:Akashi Kaikyo Bridge|Akashi Kaikyo Bridge]] (the second-longest [[suspension bridge]] in the world) to [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji Island]], from there via the [[:en:Ōnaruto Bridge|Ōnaruto Bridge]] to [[:en:Ōge-jima|Ōge-jima]] ([[:en:Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) beyond the 1.3-kilometer wide [[:en:Naruto Strait|Naruto Strait]] and finally across the Muya Bridge to [[Shikoku]]. ====Seto Chuo Highway==== The Great Seto Bridge connects Okayama Prefecture with Kagawa Prefecture since 1988. It consists of a total of six two-storey bridges, whose lower floors are used by the railway ([[:en:Japan Railways Group|Japan Railways Group]]). The high speed [[Shinkansen]] does not go to or on Shikoku. ====Nishiseto Highway / Shimanami Highway==== This is the first of three intersections of the Seto Inland Sea. Construction started in 1975, but was fully completed in 1999. It connects the Nishiseto- [[:en:Onomichi|Onomichi]] Highway in Hiroshima Prefecture with a total of ten bridges and several smaller islands with Imabari in [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime Prefecture]]. Approximately 100,000 people live on those islands. The bridges are: Shin Onomichi Bridge, [[:en:Innoshima Bridge|Innoshima Bridge]], Ikuchi Bridge, [[Tatara Bridge]], Ōmishima Bridge, the two Ōshima bridges and the three Kurushima Kaikyo bridges. The [[:en:Kurushima Kaikyō Bridge|Kurushima Kaikyō Bridge]] connects the island of [[:en:Ōshima (Ehime)|Ōshima]] to the main island of [[Shikoku]]. ====Other bridges==== The [[:en:Akinada Tobishima Kaido|Akinada Tobishima Kaido]] route connects seven of the western [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]] to mainland Honshu near [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure, Hiroshima]]. ===Maritime=== Seto Naikai Pilots Area provides compulsory [[:en:maritime pilot|maritime piloting]] for vessels over 10,000 tones, it was divided into sections of Bisanseto and sections of [[:en:Kurushima|Kurushima]], connecting [[:en:Kanmon Channel|Kanmon Channel]] Piloting Area and [[:en:Osaka Bay|Osaka Bay]] Piloting Area.{{cite web|title=固有の特徴を持つ内海水先区に精通したスペシャリスト|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/common/001415160.pdf|publisher=国土交通省|year=2021}}{{cite web|title=水先区・強制水先の範囲に関する参考資料|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/kaiji/mizusaki/003/sankoushiryou2.pdf|publisher=国土交通省}} ==Major tourist sites== [[File:Mount_Ishizuchi.jpg|thumb|220px|[[:en:Mount Ishizuchi|Mount Ishizuchi]]]] [[File:Mimosusodouzou.JPG|thumb|220px|[[Mimosusogawa Park]] ([[:ja:みもすそ川公園]]) in [[Shimonoseki]]]] The coastal area of the Seto Inland Sea is one of the most famous tourist destinations in Japan. Even before Japan opened to foreigners in the middle of the 19th century, the sea's beauty was praised and introduced to the Western world by those who visited Japan, including [[:en:Philipp Franz von Siebold|Philipp Franz von Siebold]], and after the country's opening, [[:en:Ferdinand von Richthofen|Ferdinand von Richthofen]] and [[Thomas Cook]]. Its coastal area, except for [[:en:Osaka Prefecture|Osaka Prefecture]] and a part of [[Wakayama Prefecture]], was appointed the {{nihongo|[[Setonaikai National Park]]|瀬戸内海国立公園|Setonaikai Kokuritsu kōen}} on March 16, 1934, as one of three oldest national parks in Japan. [[Itsukushima Shrine]], on the island of [[Itsukushima]] in the city of [[:en:Hatsukaichi|Hatsukaichi]], is a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]] and one of the most famous Japanese sites outside [[Tokyo]] and [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. [[Shōdoshima]], nicknamed the "island of olives", and the [[:en:Naruto whirlpools|Naruto whirlpools]] are two other well-known tourist sites. Neighboring locations like [[:en:Kotohira, Kagawa|Kotohira]] and [[:en:Okayama|Okayama]] are often combined with the tour of the Setouchi region. Some historic sites, including Yashima in [[Takamatsu, Kagawa|Takamatsu]] and [[:en:Kurashiki|Kurashiki]], also attract many visitors. [[:en:Hiroshima|Hiroshima]] is the neighbor city to Itsukushima Shrine and another UNESCO World Heritage Site because of [[:en:Atomic bomb|Atomic bomb]] damage in 1945. Idol Unit [[STU48]] operate on a cruise on the Setuchi. The eastern end of the Sea is now famous for the [[Setouchi Triennale]] set up in 2010 with the next event happening in 2022. Some of this takes place on the island of [[Naoshima]], known colloquially as the art island, and the home of several permanent museums. At the far eastern extremity, as the Sea meets the Pacific Ocean, are the [[:en:Naruto whirlpools|Naruto whirlpools]] that can be reached by sight-seeing boats. The [[Shiwaku Islands]] are a defined group numbering 28 that can be reached by ferry boat from [[:en:Marugame|Marugame]]. Here [[Richard Henry Brunton]] built one of his lighthouses that can still be seen, and the grave of [[FRank Toovey Lake]], a young midshipman in his survey party has become famous. In the central area of Seto Inland Sea is [[:en:Mount Ishizuchi|Mount Ishizuchi]] on [[Shikoku]]. It is the highest mountain in western Japan and the highest mountain in [[Shikoku]]. In the western end of the Sea is [[Mimosusogawa Park]] ([[:ja:みもすそ川公園]]) in [[Shimonoseki]]. It commemorates the final stage of the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]] between the feudal [[Taira clan]] and [[Minamoto clan]] (1180–1185). ==Literature== Some sites along the Seto Inland Sea were featured in eighth-century Japanese literature, both in prose and in verse, including {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Nihon Shoki]]}}, and {{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Man'yōshū|Man'yōshū]]}}. Since some sites were used as places of exile, their feeling and landscape were evoked in [[Waka (poetry)|waka]]. In fiction, in ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', Genji fled from Kyoto and resided in Suma (now a part of [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]) and [[:en:Akashi, Hyōgo|Akashi]] for two years. In medieval literature, because of the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], the Seto Inland Sea is one of the important backgrounds of ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'', particularly in its latter part. In the Western world, [[:en:Donald Richie|Donald Richie]] wrote a literary nonfiction travelogue called ''[[The Inland Sea]]'' relating a journey along the sea, beginning from the East at Himeji and ending at Miyajima in the West, close to Hiroshima, going from island to island, exploring the landscape, meeting and discussing with local people, as well as musing on Japanese culture, the nature of travel and of identity, and his own personal sense of identity. In 1991, filmmakers [[:en:Lucille Carra|Lucille Carra]] and Brian Cotnoir produced a film version of Richie's book, which further explored the region through interviews and images photographed by Hiro Narita. Produced by Travelfilm Company and adapted by Carra, the film won numerous awards, including Best Documentary at the Hawaii International Film Festival (1991) and the Earthwatch Film Award. It screened at the Sundance Film Festival in 1992.[https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E0CE2DF143DF934A25755C0A964958260 NY Times review] [[:en:Koushun Takami|Koushun Takami]]'s novel ''[[:en:Battle Royale (novel)|Battle Royale]]'' took place on a fictional island in the Seto Inland Sea. A critical plot element of the Japanese series ''[[:en:Fafner in the Azure|Fafner in the Azure]]'' is an alien life form discovered at the bottom of this sea known as the Seto Inland Sea Mir. Author and literary critic Amy Chavez's ''[[The Widow, the Priest and the Octopus Hunter: Discovering a Lost Way of Life on a Secluded Japanese Island]]'' is an account of the author's firsthand experience living among and interacting with the residents of Shiraishi. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * [http://www.env.go.jp/park/setonaikai/ Seto Inland Sea National Park Official {{Short description|Japanese Inland Sea}} {{more citations needed|date=May 2010}} {{Infobox body of water | name = Seto Inland Sea | image = Seto Inland Sea.jpg | caption = View of the Seto Inland Sea from [[Itsukushima|Miyajima island]] | image_bathymetry = Seto-Inland-Sea-Photo.jpg | caption_bathymetry = The Inland Sea and its major straits | location = [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] | coords = {{coord|34|10|N|133|20|E|region:JP_type:waterbody_scale:1300000|display=inline,title}} | type = [[Sea]] | inflow = |pushpin_map=Japan | outflow = | catchment = | basin_countries = [[:en:Japan|Japan]] | length = | width = | area = {{convert|23203|km2|sqmi|-2|abbr=on}} | depth = {{convert|38|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} | max-depth = | volume = | reference = }} The {{nihongo|'''Seto Inland Sea'''|瀬戸内海|Seto Naikai}}, sometimes shortened to the '''Inland Sea''', is the body of water separating [[Honshu]], [[Shikoku]], and [[Kyushu]], three of the four main islands of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It serves as a [[waterway]] connecting the [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] to the [[Sea of Japan]]. It connects to [[:en:Osaka Bay|Osaka Bay]] and provides a sea transport link to industrial centers in the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]], including [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]] and [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]. Before the construction of the [[San'yō Main Line]], it was the main transportation link between Kansai and Kyūshū. [[Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi]], [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama]], [[:en:Hyōgo Prefecture|Hyōgo]], [[:en:Osaka Prefecture|Osaka]], [[Wakayama Prefecture|Wakayama]], [[:en:Kagawa Prefecture|Kagawa]], [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime]], [[Tokushima Prefecture|Tokushima]], [[:en:Fukuoka Prefecture|Fukuoka]], and [[:en:Ōita Prefecture|Ōita]] prefectures have coastlines on the Seto Inland Sea; the cities of [[:en:Hiroshima|Hiroshima]], [[:en:Iwakuni|Iwakuni]], [[Takamatsu]], and [[:en:Matsuyama|Matsuyama]] are also located on it. The [[Setouchi region]] encompasses the sea and surrounding coastal areas. The region is known for its moderate climate, with a stable year-round temperature and relatively low rainfall levels. The sea is famous for its periodic {{nihongo|[[red tide]]s|赤潮|akashio}} caused by dense groupings of certain [[:en:phytoplankton|phytoplankton]] that result in the death of large numbers of fish. Since the 1980s, the sea's northern and southern shores have been connected by the three routes of the [[:en:Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project|Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project]], including the [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]], which serves both railroad and automobile traffic. ==Extent== The [[:en:International Hydrographic Organization|International Hydrographic Organization]]'s definition of the limits of the Seto Inland Sea (published in 1953) is as follows:{{cite web|url=https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/standards/s-23/S-23_Ed3_1953_EN.pdf|title=Limits of Oceans and Seas, 3rd edition|year=1953|publisher=International Hydrographic Organization|access-date=28 December 2020}}
''On the West.'' The southeastern limit of the Japan Sea [In [[:en:Kanmon Straits|Shimonoseki-kaikyo]]. A line running from Nagoya Saki (130°49'E) in [[Kyushu|Kyûsû]] through the islands of Uma Sima and Muture Simia (33°58',5N) to Murasaki Hana (34°01'N) in [[Honshu|Honsyû]]]. ''On the East ([[:en:Kii Channel|Kii Suidô]]).'' A line running from Takura Saki (34°16'N) in Honsyû to Oishi Hana in the island of [[:en:Awaji Island|Awazi]], through this island to Sio Saki (34°11'N) and on to Oiso Saki in [[Shikoku|Sikoku]]. ''On the South ([[:en:Bungo Channel|Bungo Suidô]]).'' A line joining Sada Misaki (33°20'N) in Sikoku and Seki Saki in Kyûsyû.
The range of the Seto Inland Sea by the Territorial Sea Law ([[:ja:領海及び接続水域に関する法律|領海及び接続水域に関する法律]]) is {{convert|19,700|km2|mi2|abbr=on}}. The range of the Seto Inland Sea according to the Setouchi Law and the Setouchi Law Enforcement Order is {{convert|21,827|km2|mi2|abbr=on}}. ==Geographical features== [[File:Chugoku-Region-Shikoku-Japan-ISS-Space.png|thumb|220px|The Seto Inland Sea with [[Shikoku]] and [[:en:Chūgoku region|Chūgoku]] from the [[:en:International Space Station|ISS]]]] [[File:Setouchi.jpg|thumb|220px|The beauty of the islands of the Seto Inland Sea, [[Suō-Ōshima]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]]] The Seto Inland Sea is 450 km (280 mi) long from east to west. The width from south to north varies from 15 to 55 km (10 to 34 mi). In most places, the water is relatively shallow. The average depth is 38 m (125 ft); the greatest depth is 105 m (344 ft).{{cite web|title=Inland Sea|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/288431/Inland-Sea|publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica Online|access-date=22 February 2013}} Hydrologically, Seto Inland Sea is not a true [[:en:inland sea|inland sea]], being neither an [[:en:epeiric|epeiric]] body of water like [[:en:Hudson Bay|Hudson Bay]] nor an isolated [[:en:endorheic basin|endorheic basin]] like the [[:en:Caspian Sea|Caspian Sea]]. Rather, it is actually a [[:en:marginal sea|marginal sea]]: a division of a wider ocean (in this case the Pacific) which is partially enclosed by islands, archipelagos, or peninsulas (here, the Japanese Home Islands), adjacent to or widely open to the open ocean at the surface. The [[:en:Naruto Strait|Naruto Strait]] connects the eastern part of the Seto Inland Sea to the [[:en:Kii Channel|Kii Channel]], which in turn connects to the Pacific. The western part of the Seto Inland Sea connects to the Sea of Japan through the [[:en:Kanmon Straits|Kanmon Straits]] and to the Pacific through the [[:en:Bungo Channel|Bungo Channel]]. Each part of the Seto Inland Sea has a separate name in Japanese. For example, {{nihongo|''Iyo-nada''|伊予灘}} refers to the strait between Ehime, Yamaguchi, and Ōita prefectures in the western portion of the sea; {{nihongo|''Aki-nada''|安芸灘}} is the open expanse west of the [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]], near Hiroshima prefecture; and {{nihongo|''Suō-nada''|周防灘}} refers to the expanse between Yamaguchi prefecture and [[Suō-Ōshima]]. These areas are sometimes styled Iyonada, Akinada, and Suonada. There are also many straits located between the major islands, as well as a number of smaller ones that pass between islands or connect the Seto Inland Sea to other seas or the [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific]]. Almost 3,000 islands are located in the Seto Inland Sea. The largest island is [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji-shima]], and the second largest is [[Shōdo Island|Shōdo-shima]]. Many of the smaller islands are uninhabited. ===Major islands=== *Eastern part: [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji Island]], [[Shōdo Island]], Ieshima Islands, [[Naoshima]] Islands, [[Shiwaku Islands]], [[Yumeshima]] *Central part: [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]] (including [[:en:Ōmishima|Ōmishima]], [[:en:Innoshima, Hiroshima|Innoshima]]), [[Itsukushima]] (popularly known as Miyajima), [[Hinase Islands]], [[:en:Kasaoka Islands|Kasaoka Islands]] *Western part: [[Suō-Ōshima]], [[Uwakai Islands]], [[:en:Hashira Island|Hashira-jima]] Islands. ==Fauna== Over 500 marine species are known to live in the Seto Inland Sea. Examples are the [[:en:Ayu sweetfish|ayu]], an [[:en:fish migration|amphidromous]] fish, [[:en:horseshoe crab|horseshoe crab]], [[:en:finless porpoise|finless porpoise]], and [[:en:great white shark|great white shark]], which has occasionally attacked people in the Seto Inland Sea. In the past, [[whale]]s entered the sea to feed or breed, however because of [[whaling]] and pollution, they are rarely seen. ==History== [[Image:ItsukushimaTorii7492.jpg|thumb|220px|Seto Inland Sea seen from the [[Torii]] of [[Itsukushima Shrine]]]] During the last [[:en:ice age|ice age]], the [[sea level]] was lower than today. After the ice age, sea water poured into a basin between the [[:en:Chūgoku|Chūgoku]] mountains and [[Shikoku]] mountains and formed the Seto Inland Sea as it is known today. From ancient times, the Seto Inland Sea served as a main transport line between its coastal areas, including what is today the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]] and [[Kyushu]]. It was also a main transport line between Japan and other countries, including Korea and China. Even after the creation of major highways such as the [[:en:Nankaidō|Nankaidō]] and [[San'yōdō]], the Seto Inland Sea remained a major transport route. There are records that some foreign emissaries from China and Korea sailed on the Seto Inland Sea. The importance of water traffic gave rise to private navies in the region. In many documents, these navies were called {{nihongo|''suigun''|水軍||"water army"}}, or simply pirates. Sometimes they were considered to be public enemies, but in most cases they were granted the right to self-governance as a result of their strength. During the feudal period, ''suigun'' seized power in most coastal areas. The Kono in [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo Province]] (today [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime Prefecture]]) and [[:en:Kobayakawa clan|Kobayakawa]] (later [[:en:Mōri clan|Mōri]]) in [[:en:Aki Province|Aki Province]] (today a part of [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]]) clans were two of the more famous ''suigun'' lords. In the 12th century, [[Taira no Kiyomori]] planned to move the capital from [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] to the coastal village of Fukuhara (today [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]) to promote trade between Japan and the [[Song dynasty]] of China. This transfer was unsuccessful, and soon after Kyoto became the capital again. Later, the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] took place off the coast of present-day Takamatsu. In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the Seto Inland Sea was one of the busiest transport lines in Japan. It was a part of a navigational route around Japan's islands via the Sea of Japan. Many ships navigated from its coastal areas to the area along the Sea of Japan. Major ports in the Edo period were Osaka, Sakai, Shimotsui, [[Ushimado]], and Tomonoura. The Seto Inland Sea also served many ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' in the western area of Japan as their route to and from [[:en:Edo|Edo]], to fulfill their obligations under ''[[sankin-kōtai]]''. Many used ships from Osaka. Thanks to transport through the Seto Inland Sea, Osaka became the economic center of Japan. Each [[:en:Han (Japan)|''han'']] had an office called ''Ozakayashiki'' in Osaka. These ''Ozakayashiki'' were among Japan's earliest forms of banks, facilitating domestic trade and helping to organize the income of the ''daimyo'', which was in the form of ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'', giant bales of rice. The Seto Inland Sea was also part of the official Chosendentsushi route, bringing Korean emissaries to the shogunate. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], the coastal cities along the Seto Inland Sea were rapidly industrialized. One of the headquarters of the [[:en:Imperial Japanese Navy|Japanese Navy]] was built in the town of [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure]]. Since the Meiji period, development of land transport has been reducing the importance of the Seto Inland Sea as a transport line. Remarkable land transportation innovations include the [[San'yō Main Line|San'yō Main Railroad Line]] in Honshū and the [[Yosan Main Railroad Line]] in Shikoku (both completed before [[World War II]]) and three series of bridges connecting Honshū and Shikoku (completed in the late 20th century). The Seto Inland Sea is still used, however, by an international cargo transport line and several local transport lines connecting Honshū with Shikoku and Kyūshū. ==Industry== Major cities with heavy industrial activity on the coast of the Seto Inland Sea include Osaka, Kobe, and Hiroshima. Smaller scale manufacturing and industry can also be found in [[:en:Kurashiki|Kurashiki]], [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure]], [[:en:Fukuyama, Hiroshima|Fukuyama]], and [[Ube, Yamaguchi|Ube]] in Honshū, and [[Sakaide, Kagawa|Sakaide]], [[:en:Imabari, Ehime|Imabari]], and [[:en:Niihama|Niihama]] in Shikoku. Major industries include [[steel]] production, vehicle manufacture, ship building, textiles, and since the 1960s, oil refining and chemical products. [[:en:Imabari Shipbuilding|Imabari Shipbuilding]], Japan's largest ship building company, has its headquarters and some of its yards in [[:en:Imabari, Ehime|Imabari, Ehime]] Prefecture. Thanks to the moderate climate and beautiful landscape, fishing, agriculture, and tourism bring a lot of income to the area as well. == Transport == [[Image:Map_of_Honshu-Shikoku_Bridge_Project.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.5|Major highways in the Seto Inland Sea. Yellow: Kobe-Awaji-Naruto. Green: Seto-Ōhashi. Red: [[:en:Nishiseto Expressway|Nishiseto Expressway]].]] [[File:Wake behind a ferry.jpg|thumb|220px|KURE-MATSUYAMA ferry, Seto Inland Sea 2017]] Today the Seto Inland Sea serves its coastal areas mainly for two purposes: first, international or domestic cargo transportation, and second, local transportation between coastal areas and islands on the sea. Major ports are Kobe, Okayama, [[:en:Port of Takamatsu|Takamatsu]], Tokushima, Matsuyama, and Hiroshima. Historically, the Seto Inland Sea as transport line served four coastal areas: Kansai, Chūgoku, Shikoku, and eastern Kyūshū. The Seto Inland Sea provided each of these regions with local transportation and connected each region to the others and far areas, including the coastal area of the Sea of Japan, Korea, and China. After Kobe port was founded in 1868 to serve foreign ships, the Seto Inland Sea became a major international waterway with connection to the Pacific. Development of land transportation shifted the travel between east and west — that is, between Honshū and Kyūshū — to railroad and road transport. Two coastal railways, San'yō Main Line in Honshū and Yosan Main Line, were built. Those railway lines stimulated the local economy and once invoked a rail mania. Many short railroads were planned to connect a certain station of those two lines and a local seaport on the Seto Inland Sea, and some of them were actually built. The Ministry of Railroads, later the [[:en:Japanese National Railways|Japanese National Railways]] and then [[Shikoku Railway Company]], ran some train ferry lines between Honshū and Shikoku including the line between Uno Station (Tamano) and [[Takamatsu Station (Kagawa)|Takamatsu Station]] (Takamatsu). When the [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]] was finished and began to serve the two coastal areas, that ferry line was abolished. ===Highways and bridges=== [[File:Akashi_Bridge.JPG|thumb|220px|right|[[:en:Akashi Kaikyō Bridge|Akashi Kaikyō Bridge]]]] The main islands Honshū and Shikoku are connected by three series of bridges since the late 1980s. This improves land transportation between the connected islands. These series of bridges, collectively known as the [[:en:Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project|Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project]], are, from east to west, [[:en:Akashi Kaikyo Bridge|Akashi Kaikyo Bridge]], [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]], and [[:en:Nishiseto Expressway|Nishiseto Expressway]]. ====Kobe-Awaji-Naruto Highway==== The easternmost highway was built between 1976 and 1998. It leads from [[Akashi,_Hyōgo|Akashi]] ([[:en:Hyōgo Prefecture|Hyōgo Prefecture]]) on the [[:en:Akashi Kaikyo Bridge|Akashi Kaikyo Bridge]] (the second-longest [[suspension bridge]] in the world) to [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji Island]], from there via the [[:en:Ōnaruto Bridge|Ōnaruto Bridge]] to [[:en:Ōge-jima|Ōge-jima]] ([[:en:Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) beyond the 1.3-kilometer wide [[:en:Naruto Strait|Naruto Strait]] and finally across the Muya Bridge to [[Shikoku]]. ====Seto Chuo Highway==== The Great Seto Bridge connects Okayama Prefecture with Kagawa Prefecture since 1988. It consists of a total of six two-storey bridges, whose lower floors are used by the railway ([[:en:Japan Railways Group|Japan Railways Group]]). The high speed [[Shinkansen]] does not go to or on Shikoku. ====Nishiseto Highway / Shimanami Highway==== This is the first of three intersections of the Seto Inland Sea. Construction started in 1975, but was fully completed in 1999. It connects the Nishiseto- [[:en:Onomichi|Onomichi]] Highway in Hiroshima Prefecture with a total of ten bridges and several smaller islands with Imabari in [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime Prefecture]]. Approximately 100,000 people live on those islands. The bridges are: Shin Onomichi Bridge, [[:en:Innoshima Bridge|Innoshima Bridge]], Ikuchi Bridge, [[Tatara Bridge]], Ōmishima Bridge, the two Ōshima bridges and the three Kurushima Kaikyo bridges. The [[:en:Kurushima Kaikyō Bridge|Kurushima Kaikyō Bridge]] connects the island of [[:en:Ōshima (Ehime)|Ōshima]] to the main island of [[Shikoku]]. ====Other bridges==== The [[:en:Akinada Tobishima Kaido|Akinada Tobishima Kaido]] route connects seven of the western [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]] to mainland Honshu near [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure, Hiroshima]]. ===Maritime=== Seto Naikai Pilots Area provides compulsory [[:en:maritime pilot|maritime piloting]] for vessels over 10,000 tones, it was divided into sections of Bisanseto and sections of [[:en:Kurushima|Kurushima]], connecting [[:en:Kanmon Channel|Kanmon Channel]] Piloting Area and [[:en:Osaka Bay|Osaka Bay]] Piloting Area.{{cite web|title=固有の特徴を持つ内海水先区に精通したスペシャリスト|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/common/001415160.pdf|publisher=国土交通省|year=2021}}{{cite web|title=水先区・強制水先の範囲に関する参考資料|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/kaiji/mizusaki/003/sankoushiryou2.pdf|publisher=国土交通省}} ==Major tourist sites== [[File:Mount_Ishizuchi.jpg|thumb|220px|[[:en:Mount Ishizuchi|Mount Ishizuchi]]]] [[File:Mimosusodouzou.JPG|thumb|220px|[[Mimosusogawa Park]] ([[:ja:みもすそ川公園]]) in [[Shimonoseki]]]] The coastal area of the Seto Inland Sea is one of the most famous tourist destinations in Japan. Even before Japan opened to foreigners in the middle of the 19th century, the sea's beauty was praised and introduced to the Western world by those who visited Japan, including [[:en:Philipp Franz von Siebold|Philipp Franz von Siebold]], and after the country's opening, [[:en:Ferdinand von Richthofen|Ferdinand von Richthofen]] and [[Thomas Cook]]. Its coastal area, except for [[:en:Osaka Prefecture|Osaka Prefecture]] and a part of [[Wakayama Prefecture]], was appointed the {{nihongo|[[Setonaikai National Park]]|瀬戸内海国立公園|Setonaikai Kokuritsu kōen}} on March 16, 1934, as one of three oldest national parks in Japan. [[Itsukushima Shrine]], on the island of [[Itsukushima]] in the city of [[:en:Hatsukaichi|Hatsukaichi]], is a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]] and one of the most famous Japanese sites outside [[Tokyo]] and [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. [[Shōdoshima]], nicknamed the "island of olives", and the [[:en:Naruto whirlpools|Naruto whirlpools]] are two other well-known tourist sites. Neighboring locations like [[:en:Kotohira, Kagawa|Kotohira]] and [[:en:Okayama|Okayama]] are often combined with the tour of the Setouchi region. Some historic sites, including Yashima in [[Takamatsu, Kagawa|Takamatsu]] and [[:en:Kurashiki|Kurashiki]], also attract many visitors. [[:en:Hiroshima|Hiroshima]] is the neighbor city to Itsukushima Shrine and another UNESCO World Heritage Site because of [[:en:Atomic bomb|Atomic bomb]] damage in 1945. Idol Unit [[:en:STU48|STU48]] operate on a cruise on the Setuchi. The eastern end of the Sea is now famous for the [[Setouchi Triennale]] set up in 2010 with the next event happening in 2022. Some of this takes place on the island of [[Naoshima]], known colloquially as the art island, and the home of several permanent museums. At the far eastern extremity, as the Sea meets the Pacific Ocean, are the [[:en:Naruto whirlpools|Naruto whirlpools]] that can be reached by sight-seeing boats. The [[Shiwaku Islands]] are a defined group numbering 28 that can be reached by ferry boat from [[:en:Marugame|Marugame]]. Here [[Richard Henry Brunton]] built one of his lighthouses that can still be seen, and the grave of [[FRank Toovey Lake]], a young midshipman in his survey party has become famous. In the central area of Seto Inland Sea is [[:en:Mount Ishizuchi|Mount Ishizuchi]] on [[Shikoku]]. It is the highest mountain in western Japan and the highest mountain in [[Shikoku]]. In the western end of the Sea is [[Mimosusogawa Park]] ([[:ja:みもすそ川公園]]) in [[Shimonoseki]]. It commemorates the final stage of the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]] between the feudal [[Taira clan]] and [[Minamoto clan]] (1180–1185). ==Literature== Some sites along the Seto Inland Sea were featured in eighth-century Japanese literature, both in prose and in verse, including {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Nihon Shoki]]}}, and {{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Man'yōshū|Man'yōshū]]}}. Since some sites were used as places of exile, their feeling and landscape were evoked in [[Waka (poetry)|waka]]. In fiction, in ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', Genji fled from Kyoto and resided in Suma (now a part of [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]) and [[:en:Akashi, Hyōgo|Akashi]] for two years. In medieval literature, because of the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], the Seto Inland Sea is one of the important backgrounds of ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'', particularly in its latter part. In the Western world, [[:en:Donald Richie|Donald Richie]] wrote a literary nonfiction travelogue called ''[[The Inland Sea]]'' relating a journey along the sea, beginning from the East at Himeji and ending at Miyajima in the West, close to Hiroshima, going from island to island, exploring the landscape, meeting and discussing with local people, as well as musing on Japanese culture, the nature of travel and of identity, and his own personal sense of identity. In 1991, filmmakers [[:en:Lucille Carra|Lucille Carra]] and Brian Cotnoir produced a film version of Richie's book, which further explored the region through interviews and images photographed by Hiro Narita. Produced by Travelfilm Company and adapted by Carra, the film won numerous awards, including Best Documentary at the Hawaii International Film Festival (1991) and the Earthwatch Film Award. It screened at the Sundance Film Festival in 1992.[https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E0CE2DF143DF934A25755C0A964958260 NY Times review] [[:en:Koushun Takami|Koushun Takami]]'s novel ''[[:en:Battle Royale (novel)|Battle Royale]]'' took place on a fictional island in the Seto Inland Sea. A critical plot element of the Japanese series ''[[:en:Fafner in the Azure|Fafner in the Azure]]'' is an alien life form discovered at the bottom of this sea known as the Seto Inland Sea Mir. Author and literary critic Amy Chavez's ''[[The Widow, the Priest and the Octopus Hunter: Discovering a Lost Way of Life on a Secluded Japanese Island]]'' is an account of the author's firsthand experience living among and interacting with the residents of Shiraishi. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * [http://www.env.go.jp/park/setonaikai/ Seto Inland Sea National Park Official {{Short description|Japanese Inland Sea}} {{more citations needed|date=May 2010}} {{Infobox body of water | name = Seto Inland Sea | image = Seto Inland Sea.jpg | caption = View of the Seto Inland Sea from [[Itsukushima|Miyajima island]] | image_bathymetry = Seto-Inland-Sea-Photo.jpg | caption_bathymetry = The Inland Sea and its major straits | location = [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] | coords = {{coord|34|10|N|133|20|E|region:JP_type:waterbody_scale:1300000|display=inline,title}} | type = [[Sea]] | inflow = |pushpin_map=Japan | outflow = | catchment = | basin_countries = [[:en:Japan|Japan]] | length = | width = | area = {{convert|23203|km2|sqmi|-2|abbr=on}} | depth = {{convert|38|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} | max-depth = | volume = | reference = }} The {{nihongo|'''Seto Inland Sea'''|瀬戸内海|Seto Naikai}}, sometimes shortened to the '''Inland Sea''', is the body of water separating [[Honshu]], [[Shikoku]], and [[Kyushu]], three of the four main islands of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. It serves as a [[waterway]] connecting the [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] to the [[Sea of Japan]]. It connects to [[:en:Osaka Bay|Osaka Bay]] and provides a sea transport link to industrial centers in the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]], including [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]] and [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]. Before the construction of the [[San'yō Main Line]], it was the main transportation link between Kansai and Kyūshū. [[Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi]], [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima]], [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama]], [[:en:Hyōgo Prefecture|Hyōgo]], [[:en:Osaka Prefecture|Osaka]], [[Wakayama Prefecture|Wakayama]], [[:en:Kagawa Prefecture|Kagawa]], [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime]], [[Tokushima Prefecture|Tokushima]], [[:en:Fukuoka Prefecture|Fukuoka]], and [[:en:Ōita Prefecture|Ōita]] prefectures have coastlines on the Seto Inland Sea; the cities of [[:en:Hiroshima|Hiroshima]], [[:en:Iwakuni|Iwakuni]], [[Takamatsu]], and [[:en:Matsuyama|Matsuyama]] are also located on it. The [[Setouchi region]] encompasses the sea and surrounding coastal areas. The region is known for its moderate climate, with a stable year-round temperature and relatively low rainfall levels. The sea is famous for its periodic {{nihongo|[[red tide]]s|赤潮|akashio}} caused by dense groupings of certain [[:en:phytoplankton|phytoplankton]] that result in the death of large numbers of fish. Since the 1980s, the sea's northern and southern shores have been connected by the three routes of the [[:en:Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project|Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project]], including the [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]], which serves both railroad and automobile traffic. ==Extent== The [[:en:International Hydrographic Organization|International Hydrographic Organization]]'s definition of the limits of the Seto Inland Sea (published in 1953) is as follows:{{cite web|url=https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/standards/s-23/S-23_Ed3_1953_EN.pdf|title=Limits of Oceans and Seas, 3rd edition|year=1953|publisher=International Hydrographic Organization|access-date=28 December 2020}}
''On the West.'' The southeastern limit of the Japan Sea [In [[:en:Kanmon Straits|Shimonoseki-kaikyo]]. A line running from Nagoya Saki (130°49'E) in [[Kyushu|Kyûsû]] through the islands of Uma Sima and Muture Simia (33°58',5N) to Murasaki Hana (34°01'N) in [[Honshu|Honsyû]]]. ''On the East ([[:en:Kii Channel|Kii Suidô]]).'' A line running from Takura Saki (34°16'N) in Honsyû to Oishi Hana in the island of [[:en:Awaji Island|Awazi]], through this island to Sio Saki (34°11'N) and on to Oiso Saki in [[Shikoku|Sikoku]]. ''On the South ([[:en:Bungo Channel|Bungo Suidô]]).'' A line joining Sada Misaki (33°20'N) in Sikoku and Seki Saki in Kyûsyû.
The range of the Seto Inland Sea by the Territorial Sea Law ([[:ja:領海及び接続水域に関する法律|領海及び接続水域に関する法律]]) is {{convert|19,700|km2|mi2|abbr=on}}. The range of the Seto Inland Sea according to the Setouchi Law and the Setouchi Law Enforcement Order is {{convert|21,827|km2|mi2|abbr=on}}. ==Geographical features== [[File:Chugoku-Region-Shikoku-Japan-ISS-Space.png|thumb|220px|The Seto Inland Sea with [[Shikoku]] and [[:en:Chūgoku region|Chūgoku]] from the [[:en:International Space Station|ISS]]]] [[File:Setouchi.jpg|thumb|220px|The beauty of the islands of the Seto Inland Sea, [[Suō-Ōshima]], [[Yamaguchi Prefecture]]]] The Seto Inland Sea is 450 km (280 mi) long from east to west. The width from south to north varies from 15 to 55 km (10 to 34 mi). In most places, the water is relatively shallow. The average depth is 38 m (125 ft); the greatest depth is 105 m (344 ft).{{cite web|title=Inland Sea|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/288431/Inland-Sea|publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica Online|access-date=22 February 2013}} Hydrologically, Seto Inland Sea is not a true [[:en:inland sea|inland sea]], being neither an [[:en:epeiric|epeiric]] body of water like [[:en:Hudson Bay|Hudson Bay]] nor an isolated [[:en:endorheic basin|endorheic basin]] like the [[:en:Caspian Sea|Caspian Sea]]. Rather, it is actually a [[:en:marginal sea|marginal sea]]: a division of a wider ocean (in this case the Pacific) which is partially enclosed by islands, archipelagos, or peninsulas (here, the Japanese Home Islands), adjacent to or widely open to the open ocean at the surface. The [[:en:Naruto Strait|Naruto Strait]] connects the eastern part of the Seto Inland Sea to the [[:en:Kii Channel|Kii Channel]], which in turn connects to the Pacific. The western part of the Seto Inland Sea connects to the Sea of Japan through the [[:en:Kanmon Straits|Kanmon Straits]] and to the Pacific through the [[:en:Bungo Channel|Bungo Channel]]. Each part of the Seto Inland Sea has a separate name in Japanese. For example, {{nihongo|''Iyo-nada''|伊予灘}} refers to the strait between Ehime, Yamaguchi, and Ōita prefectures in the western portion of the sea; {{nihongo|''Aki-nada''|安芸灘}} is the open expanse west of the [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]], near Hiroshima prefecture; and {{nihongo|''Suō-nada''|周防灘}} refers to the expanse between Yamaguchi prefecture and [[Suō-Ōshima]]. These areas are sometimes styled Iyonada, Akinada, and Suonada. There are also many straits located between the major islands, as well as a number of smaller ones that pass between islands or connect the Seto Inland Sea to other seas or the [[:en:Pacific Ocean|Pacific]]. Almost 3,000 islands are located in the Seto Inland Sea. The largest island is [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji-shima]], and the second largest is [[Shōdo Island|Shōdo-shima]]. Many of the smaller islands are uninhabited. ===Major islands=== *Eastern part: [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji Island]], [[Shōdo Island]], Ieshima Islands, [[Naoshima]] Islands, [[Shiwaku Islands]], [[Yumeshima]] *Central part: [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]] (including [[:en:Ōmishima|Ōmishima]], [[:en:Innoshima, Hiroshima|Innoshima]]), [[Itsukushima]] (popularly known as Miyajima), [[Hinase Islands]], [[:en:Kasaoka Islands|Kasaoka Islands]] *Western part: [[Suō-Ōshima]], [[Uwakai Islands]], [[:en:Hashira Island|Hashira-jima]] Islands. ==Fauna== Over 500 marine species are known to live in the Seto Inland Sea. Examples are the [[:en:Ayu sweetfish|ayu]], an [[:en:fish migration|amphidromous]] fish, [[:en:horseshoe crab|horseshoe crab]], [[:en:finless porpoise|finless porpoise]], and [[:en:great white shark|great white shark]], which has occasionally attacked people in the Seto Inland Sea. In the past, [[whale]]s entered the sea to feed or breed, however because of [[whaling]] and pollution, they are rarely seen. ==History== [[Image:ItsukushimaTorii7492.jpg|thumb|220px|Seto Inland Sea seen from the [[Torii]] of [[Itsukushima Shrine]]]] During the last [[:en:ice age|ice age]], the [[sea level]] was lower than today. After the ice age, sea water poured into a basin between the [[:en:Chūgoku|Chūgoku]] mountains and [[Shikoku]] mountains and formed the Seto Inland Sea as it is known today. From ancient times, the Seto Inland Sea served as a main transport line between its coastal areas, including what is today the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]] and [[Kyushu]]. It was also a main transport line between Japan and other countries, including Korea and China. Even after the creation of major highways such as the [[:en:Nankaidō|Nankaidō]] and [[San'yōdō]], the Seto Inland Sea remained a major transport route. There are records that some foreign emissaries from China and Korea sailed on the Seto Inland Sea. The importance of water traffic gave rise to private navies in the region. In many documents, these navies were called {{nihongo|''suigun''|水軍||"water army"}}, or simply pirates. Sometimes they were considered to be public enemies, but in most cases they were granted the right to self-governance as a result of their strength. During the feudal period, ''suigun'' seized power in most coastal areas. The Kono in [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo Province]] (today [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime Prefecture]]) and [[:en:Kobayakawa clan|Kobayakawa]] (later [[:en:Mōri clan|Mōri]]) in [[:en:Aki Province|Aki Province]] (today a part of [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]]) clans were two of the more famous ''suigun'' lords. In the 12th century, [[Taira no Kiyomori]] planned to move the capital from [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] to the coastal village of Fukuhara (today [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]) to promote trade between Japan and the [[Song dynasty]] of China. This transfer was unsuccessful, and soon after Kyoto became the capital again. Later, the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] took place off the coast of present-day Takamatsu. In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the Seto Inland Sea was one of the busiest transport lines in Japan. It was a part of a navigational route around Japan's islands via the Sea of Japan. Many ships navigated from its coastal areas to the area along the Sea of Japan. Major ports in the Edo period were Osaka, Sakai, Shimotsui, [[Ushimado]], and Tomonoura. The Seto Inland Sea also served many ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' in the western area of Japan as their route to and from [[:en:Edo|Edo]], to fulfill their obligations under ''[[sankin-kōtai]]''. Many used ships from Osaka. Thanks to transport through the Seto Inland Sea, Osaka became the economic center of Japan. Each [[:en:Han (Japan)|''han'']] had an office called ''Ozakayashiki'' in Osaka. These ''Ozakayashiki'' were among Japan's earliest forms of banks, facilitating domestic trade and helping to organize the income of the ''daimyo'', which was in the form of ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]'', giant bales of rice. The Seto Inland Sea was also part of the official Chosendentsushi route, bringing Korean emissaries to the shogunate. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], the coastal cities along the Seto Inland Sea were rapidly industrialized. One of the headquarters of the [[:en:Imperial Japanese Navy|Japanese Navy]] was built in the town of [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure]]. Since the Meiji period, development of land transport has been reducing the importance of the Seto Inland Sea as a transport line. Remarkable land transportation innovations include the [[San'yō Main Line|San'yō Main Railroad Line]] in Honshū and the [[Yosan Main Railroad Line]] in Shikoku (both completed before [[World War II]]) and three series of bridges connecting Honshū and Shikoku (completed in the late 20th century). The Seto Inland Sea is still used, however, by an international cargo transport line and several local transport lines connecting Honshū with Shikoku and Kyūshū. ==Industry== Major cities with heavy industrial activity on the coast of the Seto Inland Sea include Osaka, Kobe, and Hiroshima. Smaller scale manufacturing and industry can also be found in [[:en:Kurashiki|Kurashiki]], [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure]], [[:en:Fukuyama, Hiroshima|Fukuyama]], and [[Ube, Yamaguchi|Ube]] in Honshū, and [[Sakaide, Kagawa|Sakaide]], [[:en:Imabari, Ehime|Imabari]], and [[:en:Niihama|Niihama]] in Shikoku. Major industries include [[steel]] production, vehicle manufacture, ship building, textiles, and since the 1960s, oil refining and chemical products. [[:en:Imabari Shipbuilding|Imabari Shipbuilding]], Japan's largest ship building company, has its headquarters and some of its yards in [[:en:Imabari, Ehime|Imabari, Ehime]] Prefecture. Thanks to the moderate climate and beautiful landscape, fishing, agriculture, and tourism bring a lot of income to the area as well. == Transport == [[Image:Map_of_Honshu-Shikoku_Bridge_Project.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.5|Major highways in the Seto Inland Sea. Yellow: Kobe-Awaji-Naruto. Green: Seto-Ōhashi. Red: [[:en:Nishiseto Expressway|Nishiseto Expressway]].]] [[File:Wake behind a ferry.jpg|thumb|220px|KURE-MATSUYAMA ferry, Seto Inland Sea 2017]] Today the Seto Inland Sea serves its coastal areas mainly for two purposes: first, international or domestic cargo transportation, and second, local transportation between coastal areas and islands on the sea. Major ports are Kobe, Okayama, [[:en:Port of Takamatsu|Takamatsu]], Tokushima, Matsuyama, and Hiroshima. Historically, the Seto Inland Sea as transport line served four coastal areas: Kansai, Chūgoku, Shikoku, and eastern Kyūshū. The Seto Inland Sea provided each of these regions with local transportation and connected each region to the others and far areas, including the coastal area of the Sea of Japan, Korea, and China. After Kobe port was founded in 1868 to serve foreign ships, the Seto Inland Sea became a major international waterway with connection to the Pacific. Development of land transportation shifted the travel between east and west — that is, between Honshū and Kyūshū — to railroad and road transport. Two coastal railways, San'yō Main Line in Honshū and Yosan Main Line, were built. Those railway lines stimulated the local economy and once invoked a rail mania. Many short railroads were planned to connect a certain station of those two lines and a local seaport on the Seto Inland Sea, and some of them were actually built. The Ministry of Railroads, later the [[:en:Japanese National Railways|Japanese National Railways]] and then [[Shikoku Railway Company]], ran some train ferry lines between Honshū and Shikoku including the line between Uno Station (Tamano) and [[Takamatsu Station (Kagawa)|Takamatsu Station]] (Takamatsu). When the [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]] was finished and began to serve the two coastal areas, that ferry line was abolished. ===Highways and bridges=== [[File:Akashi_Bridge.JPG|thumb|220px|right|[[:en:Akashi Kaikyō Bridge|Akashi Kaikyō Bridge]]]] The main islands Honshū and Shikoku are connected by three series of bridges since the late 1980s. This improves land transportation between the connected islands. These series of bridges, collectively known as the [[:en:Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project|Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project]], are, from east to west, [[:en:Akashi Kaikyo Bridge|Akashi Kaikyo Bridge]], [[:en:Great Seto Bridge|Great Seto Bridge]], and [[:en:Nishiseto Expressway|Nishiseto Expressway]]. ====Kobe-Awaji-Naruto Highway==== The easternmost highway was built between 1976 and 1998. It leads from [[Akashi,_Hyōgo|Akashi]] ([[:en:Hyōgo Prefecture|Hyōgo Prefecture]]) on the [[:en:Akashi Kaikyo Bridge|Akashi Kaikyo Bridge]] (the second-longest [[suspension bridge]] in the world) to [[:en:Awaji Island|Awaji Island]], from there via the [[:en:Ōnaruto Bridge|Ōnaruto Bridge]] to [[:en:Ōge-jima|Ōge-jima]] ([[:en:Naruto, Tokushima|Naruto]], [[Tokushima Prefecture]]) beyond the 1.3-kilometer wide [[:en:Naruto Strait|Naruto Strait]] and finally across the Muya Bridge to [[Shikoku]]. ====Seto Chuo Highway==== The Great Seto Bridge connects Okayama Prefecture with Kagawa Prefecture since 1988. It consists of a total of six two-storey bridges, whose lower floors are used by the railway ([[:en:Japan Railways Group|Japan Railways Group]]). The high speed [[Shinkansen]] does not go to or on Shikoku. ====Nishiseto Highway / Shimanami Highway==== This is the first of three intersections of the Seto Inland Sea. Construction started in 1975, but was fully completed in 1999. It connects the Nishiseto- [[:en:Onomichi|Onomichi]] Highway in Hiroshima Prefecture with a total of ten bridges and several smaller islands with Imabari in [[:en:Ehime Prefecture|Ehime Prefecture]]. Approximately 100,000 people live on those islands. The bridges are: Shin Onomichi Bridge, [[:en:Innoshima Bridge|Innoshima Bridge]], Ikuchi Bridge, [[Tatara Bridge]], Ōmishima Bridge, the two Ōshima bridges and the three Kurushima Kaikyo bridges. The [[:en:Kurushima Kaikyō Bridge|Kurushima Kaikyō Bridge]] connects the island of [[:en:Ōshima (Ehime)|Ōshima]] to the main island of [[Shikoku]]. ====Other bridges==== The [[:en:Akinada Tobishima Kaido|Akinada Tobishima Kaido]] route connects seven of the western [[:en:Geiyo Islands|Geiyo Islands]] to mainland Honshu near [[:en:Kure, Hiroshima|Kure, Hiroshima]]. ===Maritime=== Seto Naikai Pilots Area provides compulsory [[:en:maritime pilot|maritime piloting]] for vessels over 10,000 tones, it was divided into sections of Bisanseto and sections of [[:en:Kurushima|Kurushima]], connecting [[:en:Kanmon Channel|Kanmon Channel]] Piloting Area and [[:en:Osaka Bay|Osaka Bay]] Piloting Area.{{cite web|title=固有の特徴を持つ内海水先区に精通したスペシャリスト|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/common/001415160.pdf|publisher=国土交通省|year=2021}}{{cite web|title=水先区・強制水先の範囲に関する参考資料|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/kaiji/mizusaki/003/sankoushiryou2.pdf|publisher=国土交通省}} ==Major tourist sites== [[File:Mount_Ishizuchi.jpg|thumb|220px|[[:en:Mount Ishizuchi|Mount Ishizuchi]]]] [[File:Mimosusodouzou.JPG|thumb|220px|[[Mimosusogawa Park]] ([[:ja:みもすそ川公園]]) in [[Shimonoseki]]]] The coastal area of the Seto Inland Sea is one of the most famous tourist destinations in Japan. Even before Japan opened to foreigners in the middle of the 19th century, the sea's beauty was praised and introduced to the Western world by those who visited Japan, including [[:en:Philipp Franz von Siebold|Philipp Franz von Siebold]], and after the country's opening, [[:en:Ferdinand von Richthofen|Ferdinand von Richthofen]] and [[Thomas Cook]]. Its coastal area, except for [[:en:Osaka Prefecture|Osaka Prefecture]] and a part of [[Wakayama Prefecture]], was appointed the {{nihongo|[[Setonaikai National Park]]|瀬戸内海国立公園|Setonaikai Kokuritsu kōen}} on March 16, 1934, as one of three oldest national parks in Japan. [[Itsukushima Shrine]], on the island of [[Itsukushima]] in the city of [[:en:Hatsukaichi|Hatsukaichi]], is a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]] and one of the most famous Japanese sites outside [[Tokyo]] and [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. [[Shōdoshima]], nicknamed the "island of olives", and the [[:en:Naruto whirlpools|Naruto whirlpools]] are two other well-known tourist sites. Neighboring locations like [[:en:Kotohira, Kagawa|Kotohira]] and [[:en:Okayama|Okayama]] are often combined with the tour of the Setouchi region. Some historic sites, including Yashima in [[Takamatsu, Kagawa|Takamatsu]] and [[:en:Kurashiki|Kurashiki]], also attract many visitors. [[:en:Hiroshima|Hiroshima]] is the neighbor city to Itsukushima Shrine and another UNESCO World Heritage Site because of [[:en:Atomic bomb|Atomic bomb]] damage in 1945. Idol Unit [[:en:STU48|STU48]] operate on a cruise on the Setuchi. The eastern end of the Sea is now famous for the [[Setouchi Triennale]] set up in 2010 with the next event happening in 2022. Some of this takes place on the island of [[Naoshima]], known colloquially as the art island, and the home of several permanent museums. At the far eastern extremity, as the Sea meets the Pacific Ocean, are the [[:en:Naruto whirlpools|Naruto whirlpools]] that can be reached by sight-seeing boats. The [[Shiwaku Islands]] are a defined group numbering 28 that can be reached by ferry boat from [[:en:Marugame|Marugame]]. Here [[Richard Henry Brunton]] built one of his lighthouses that can still be seen, and the grave of [[FRank Toovey Lake]], a young midshipman in his survey party has become famous. In the central area of Seto Inland Sea is [[:en:Mount Ishizuchi|Mount Ishizuchi]] on [[Shikoku]]. It is the highest mountain in western Japan and the highest mountain in [[Shikoku]]. In the western end of the Sea is [[Mimosusogawa Park]] ([[:ja:みもすそ川公園]]) in [[Shimonoseki]]. It commemorates the final stage of the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]] between the feudal [[Taira clan]] and [[Minamoto clan]] (1180–1185). ==Literature== Some sites along the Seto Inland Sea were featured in eighth-century Japanese literature, both in prose and in verse, including {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Nihon Shoki]]}}, and {{Lang|ja-latn|[[:en:Man'yōshū|Man'yōshū]]}}. Since some sites were used as places of exile, their feeling and landscape were evoked in [[:en:Waka (poetry)|waka]]. In fiction, in ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', Genji fled from Kyoto and resided in Suma (now a part of [[:en:Kobe|Kobe]]) and [[:en:Akashi, Hyōgo|Akashi]] for two years. In medieval literature, because of the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], the Seto Inland Sea is one of the important backgrounds of ''[[The Tale of the Heike]]'', particularly in its latter part. In the Western world, [[:en:Donald Richie|Donald Richie]] wrote a literary nonfiction travelogue called ''[[The Inland Sea]]'' relating a journey along the sea, beginning from the East at Himeji and ending at Miyajima in the West, close to Hiroshima, going from island to island, exploring the landscape, meeting and discussing with local people, as well as musing on Japanese culture, the nature of travel and of identity, and his own personal sense of identity. In 1991, filmmakers [[:en:Lucille Carra|Lucille Carra]] and Brian Cotnoir produced a film version of Richie's book, which further explored the region through interviews and images photographed by Hiro Narita. Produced by Travelfilm Company and adapted by Carra, the film won numerous awards, including Best Documentary at the Hawaii International Film Festival (1991) and the Earthwatch Film Award. It screened at the Sundance Film Festival in 1992.[https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E0CE2DF143DF934A25755C0A964958260 NY Times review] [[:en:Koushun Takami|Koushun Takami]]'s novel ''[[:en:Battle Royale (novel)|Battle Royale]]'' took place on a fictional island in the Seto Inland Sea. A critical plot element of the Japanese series ''[[:en:Fafner in the Azure|Fafner in the Azure]]'' is an alien life form discovered at the bottom of this sea known as the Seto Inland Sea Mir. Author and literary critic Amy Chavez's ''[[The Widow, the Priest and the Octopus Hunter: Discovering a Lost Way of Life on a Secluded Japanese Island]]'' is an account of the author's firsthand experience living among and interacting with the residents of Shiraishi. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== * [http://www.env.go.jp/park/setonaikai/ Seto Inland Sea National Park Official site] {Japanese} * [https://www.japan.travel/en/travel-directory/Setonaikai%20National%20Park/ Setonaikai National Park] - by [[:en:JNTO|JNTO]] * {{Wikivoyage-inline}} {{List of seas}} ]] ]] ]] ]] ]]
